title: The synchronous chain
summary: Why a call chain fails together: temporal coupling, multiplied availability, added latency and pool exhaustion under a traffic spike.

steps.title: The synchronous chain
body: A checkout in a typical shop calls one service, which calls the next, which calls the next. Every caller
**waits**, holding a thread, a socket and a slot in a connection pool, until the whole chain answers:
```text
browser ──> checkout-api ──> orders-api ──> billing-api ──> email-svc
waits            waits          waits          slow today (2 s)
This is **temporal coupling**: every hop must be up, and fast, *at the same moment*. Two rules fall out of it:
- **Availability multiplies.** Four hops at 99.5 % each give you about 98 %, not 99.5 %.
- **Latency adds.** The caller's response time is the sum of every hop (plus every retry).
The weakest, slowest service sets the experience for everything upstream of it, even when its work
(a confirmation email) has nothing to do with the answer the user is waiting for.

steps.prompt: Four hops are called in a row. Each one is up for the fraction of time shown. What does this print?
code: foreach (var a in hops) total *= a;
steps.explain: The chain is only up when every hop is up, so the probabilities multiply: about 15 hours of failed checkouts a month, from four services that each look fine on their own dashboard.

steps.title: Little's law: why a spike exhausts the pool
body: How many requests are **in flight** at once? Little's law: *in flight = arrival rate × time in the system*.
At 100 requests per second and 300 ms per request, 30 requests are waiting at any moment. A flash sale
brings 800 per second: now 240 are in flight, more than a pool of 200 connections or threads can hold.
New requests queue **inside your process**, their latency grows, which raises the in-flight count again:
a feedback loop that ends in timeouts everywhere upstream.
Step through it: the latency stays the same, only the traffic grows.

code: Console.WriteLine($"{r} rps x {latencyMs} ms = {inFlight} in flight ({status})");

steps.prompt: A flash sale starts. Put the cascade in the order it happens.
lines: Traffic jumps from 100 to 800 requests per second
email-svc slows down under the extra load
orders-api requests wait longer for email-svc, so more of them are in flight
orders-api exhausts its connection pool and requests queue inside the process
checkout-api calls to orders-api hit their timeout and return 504
Clients retry the failed checkouts, adding even more load
steps.explain: A slow dependency turns into a full outage through waiting, not through crashing. The retries at the end are why a cascade rarely recovers on its own.

prompt: **Symptom first.** During a sale the checkout page fails for a third of users. You find this. What is the
root cause, and what is the best fix?
code: 12:04:17 ERR orders-api    System.Threading.Tasks.TaskCanceledException: The request was canceled due to the
12:04:18 INF email-svc     smtp relay: 4812 pending, p99 9.6 s
options: Checkout waits for the confirmation email on the request path. Publish an `OrderPlaced` event and let an email consumer send it at its own pace.
The 10-second `HttpClient.Timeout` is too short. Raise it to 60 seconds.
Add three retries to the email call so transient failures recover.
explain: The stack trace shows the request thread waiting on `SendConfirmationAsync`, and the email relay is the slow
part. A longer timeout keeps threads waiting even longer, retries add load to the struggling service, and more
checkout pods just means more callers waiting on the same bottleneck. The email is not part of the answer the
user needs, so take it off the synchronous path.

steps.prompt: Which calls must stay synchronous because the user needs the answer now, and which can move behind a message?
items: Authorise the card before showing "order placed"
Show the current price of a product
Tell the warehouse to pick the order
Check the username is free on sign-up
steps.explain: Ask: does the response to *this* request depend on the result? If not, the work can happen a moment later, and a broker can hold it while the worker is slow or down.

steps.title: What a broker changes
body: Put a broker between the two sides and the caller only needs the **broker** to be up:
```text
orders-api ──publish OrderPlaced──> [ broker: email queue ] ──> email-worker (its own pace)
│                                   stores the message
└── returns 201 as soon as the broker confirms it has the message
- **email-worker down?** Messages wait in the queue; nothing upstream fails. When it comes back it drains the backlog.
- **Spike?** The queue grows instead of the error rate. Workers keep their steady rate.
- **orders-api** no longer knows the address of email-svc, only the name of the exchange or topic.
The broker must be durable and *confirm* the publish (RabbitMQ publisher confirms, Kafka `acks=all`),
otherwise "the broker has it" is a hope, not a fact. Modules 2 and 3 show how.
> **See it:** open **Labs → Messaging builder → RabbitMQ** and play the challenge *Drain the backlog*.

steps.prompt: Match each kind of coupling to what a broker does about it.
pairs: Temporal: both sides must be up at once
The broker stores the message until the consumer is back
Rate: the consumer must keep up with every peak
The queue absorbs the spike; consumers drain it at their own rate
Location: the caller knows the callee's address
The publisher only knows an exchange or topic name
Format: both sides read the same fields
Nothing: the message schema is still a contract (module 5)
steps.explain: Messaging removes the time and rate coupling, not the contract. A renamed field breaks an async consumer just as surely as a sync one, only later and more quietly.

steps.title: How many are in flight?
prompt: Write two methods based on Little's law:
- `int InFlight(int requestsPerSecond, int latencyMs)`: requests in flight at once, **rounded up**
(`InFlight(3, 500)` is `2`, not `1`: you cannot hold half a connection).
- `bool Saturated(int requestsPerSecond, int latencyMs, int poolSize)`: `true` when the in-flight count is
**greater than** the pool size.
starter: bool Saturated(int requestsPerSecond, int latencyMs, int poolSize)
solution: bool Saturated(int requestsPerSecond, int latencyMs, int poolSize)
hints: Divide as a `double` and use `Math.Ceiling`, then cast back to `int`.
template: Dojo.Eq("a 2.5 s hop at 650 rps", 1625, InFlight(650, 2500));
Dojo.Eq("exactly the pool size still fits", false, Saturated(200, 1000, 200));

steps.title: Diagnose the chain
prompt: Write the diagnosis an on-call engineer gives in the incident channel.
`string Diagnose(int rps, int poolSize, int timeoutMs, (string Name, int LatencyMs, bool NeededForReply)[] hops)`
Today every hop is called **synchronously, one after the other**.
1. `latency` = the sum of all hop latencies; `inFlight` = Little's law, rounded up (as in the last step).
2. The status, checked in this order:
- `latency > timeoutMs` → `"timeout: {latency} ms > {timeoutMs} ms"`
- `inFlight > poolSize` → `"saturated: {inFlight} in flight > pool {poolSize}"`
- otherwise → `"ok: {latency} ms, {inFlight} in flight"` and stop here.
3. If the status is not ok and some hops are **not** needed for the reply, append
`"; publish an event for: {names} (sync path {syncLatency} ms)"`: the names in the given order joined with
`", "`, and `syncLatency` the sum of the hops that **are** needed.
```text
Diagnose(400, 200, 2000, [inventory 40 needed, billing 120 needed, email 900, analytics 200])
→ "saturated: 504 in flight > pool 200; publish an event for: email, analytics (sync path 160 ms)"
starter: string Diagnose(int rps, int poolSize, int timeoutMs, (string Name, int LatencyMs, bool NeededForReply)[] hops)
solution: string Diagnose(int rps, int poolSize, int timeoutMs, (string Name, int LatencyMs, bool NeededForReply)[] hops)
else if (inFlight > poolSize) status = $"saturated: {inFlight} in flight > pool {poolSize}";
return $"{status}; publish an event for: {string.Join(", ", movable)} (sync path {sync} ms)";
hints: Compute `latency` with `hops.Sum(h => h.LatencyMs)` and return early for the ok case.
Collect `hops.Where(h => !h.NeededForReply)` names; only append the advice when there are some.
template: var dojoShop = new (string, int, bool)[] { ("inventory", 40, true), ("billing", 120, true), ("email", 900, false), ("analytics", 200, false) };
Dojo.Eq("quiet day is ok", "ok: 1260 ms, 126 in flight", Diagnose(100, 200, 2000, dojoShop));
Dojo.Eq("flash sale saturates the pool", "saturated: 504 in flight > pool 200; publish an event for: email, analytics (sync path 160 ms)", Diagnose(400, 200, 2000, dojoShop));
Dojo.Eq("timeout is checked first", "timeout: 1260 ms > 1000 ms; publish an event for: email, analytics (sync path 160 ms)", Diagnose(5000, 10, 1000, dojoShop));
var dojoAllNeeded = new (string, int, bool)[] { ("auth", 300, true), ("pricing", 900, true) };
Dojo.Eq("nothing can move off the sync path", "timeout: 1200 ms > 1000 ms", Diagnose(10, 50, 1000, dojoAllNeeded));
Dojo.Eq("saturated, nothing to move", "saturated: 600 in flight > pool 100", Diagnose(500, 100, 5000, dojoAllNeeded));
